name: The Sydney Language / Biyal-Biyal
confidence_why: Steele 2005 and Troy 1994 both read William Dawes's 1790-91 acute accents as stress marks but neither states a rule, and Steele's own examples put the accent on different syllables (second in ngarámata, final in imperatives, on the suffix -bi), so no placement can be defended; no source disagrees, but everything rests on that one colonial record and Wilkins's unpublished 1992 draft with a section headed 'stress' was not read.

catalog_quote: [Steele 2005, T6.1, p. 135] T6.1 USE AND SIGNIFICANCE OF DIACRITICS (DAWES DATA) | Diacritic | As in | Meaning | Source | Possible significance | Frequency || Acute accent | Ngarámata | younger brother | b:20:10.1 | shows stress on second syllable | hundreds. [p. 226, §8.7 Imperative:] Of over fifty examples of the imperative in the Dawes/Anon data, almost all end in a; and, where stress is indicated, it falls on the final syllable. ... The following examples show the imperative a, which generally takes the stress, as indicated by Dawes using an acute accent [á]: [p. 227] In X8.73, the stress is not shown to fall on the imperative suffix: Eereéra ... unambiguous examples of imperatives are too few in the Dawes data to attempt to draw useful conclusions in this regard. [p. 265, §9.5.1.2] -bi-ra-ng and -bi-la-ng are based on the stem-forming suffix -bi (see T8.1 and §8.4.2.3 and throughout Chapter 8), on which the stress falls (as noted by Dawes, and shown here in bold type), making them structurally distinct from -gulang. [Troy 1994, p. 25] Dawes used accute accents over all the vowels and the semi-vowel y, but only ever accented one syllable of a word. His usage suggests that he used accute to indicate stress.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (356 pp, text) with extracted text at the stated PDF pages. All three quoted passages are there verbatim: p. 157 (printed 135) §6.2 'Macrons, breves and diacritics', Table T6.1 row 'Acute accent | Ngarámata | younger brother | b:20:10.1 | shows stress on second syllable | hundreds'; p. 248 (printed 226) §8.7 Imperative: 'Of over fifty examples of the imperative in the Dawes/Anon data, almost all end in a; and, where stress is indicated, it falls on the final syllable.' followed by 'the imperative a, which generally takes the stress, as indicated by Dawes using an acute accent [á]' and, on printed p. 227, 'In X8.73, the stress is not shown to fall on the imperative suffix: Eereéra'; p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states a general word-stress rule. The language is known only from 1790s and c.1900 manuscripts. Steele reads Dawes' acute accent (hundreds of tokens, one per word) as a stress mark; his table glosses it with a second-syllable example (Nga-RA-ma-ta), while imperative forms in -a/-la carry stress on the final suffix and the stem-forming suffix -bi is stressed in -birang/-bilang. Troy 1994 (p. 25) says only that Dawes 'only ever accented one syllable of a word' and that the acute probably indicates stress. Net: stress apparently mobile and morphologically conditioned, position unresolved.
new_statements.exceptions: Steele p. 227: in X8.73 Eereéra 'throw!' the stress is not on the imperative suffix; p. 176 n. 2: wára wará 'just now' vs wará wará 'go away!' differ by 'stressing', recorded three times by Dawes.
new_statements.domain_note: All observations come from an 18th-century English officer's acute-accent marks on single words and short sentences (Dawes' notebooks a, b); Troy states phonological analysis is impossible without spoken data and her sound system is hypothetical. Word-level marks; no phrase-level analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog sydn1236 'Sydney' (ISO xdk) covers the coastal Iyora/Eora (Port Jackson, Dawes' data 1790-91) and inland Dharug/Dharruk (Mathews 1901, c.1900) varieties; Troy 1994 treats them as coastal and inland dialects of one 'Sydney Language', Steele 2005 names the language Biyal-Biyal and reconstructs it mainly from Dawes' coastal material. All stress observations above derive from Dawes' coastal notebooks.

sources.note: Ch. 6 Phonology (pp. 131-161) has no stress subsection. Table T6.1 (p. 135) glosses Dawes' acute accent as 'shows stress on second syllable' for the example Ngarámata 'younger brother', frequency 'hundreds'; p. 226 (§8.7): imperatives 'almost all end in a; and, where stress is indicated, it falls on the final syllable'; p. 265: stem-forming suffix -bi in -birang/-bilang is the syllable 'on which the stress falls (as noted by Dawes)'; p. 176 n.2: wára wará 'just now' vs wará wará 'go away!' differ by stressing. No general word-stress rule.

His usage suggests that he used accute to indicate stress.' No statement of where stress falls.
